name: Olga Dubois

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Olga, and thank you for seeing me. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for any company, union, party or government, and what you tell me is kept confidential. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Of course. I work at the benefits office in our market town, a small place above the post office, and I handle disability and carer's allowance claims. A lot of my day is face-to-face appointments, going through forms with people who can't manage them alone, and then checking the medical evidence and writing up the decision. There are seven of us, and I've been there just over five years.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about the work, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like knowing the people. I've helped the same carers for years, like a woman who looks after her son with cerebral palsy, and I know her story without opening the file. What wears me out is the computer system, honestly, it changes every year and I'm always the last to get the hang of it. I've never used any of these AI programs and I don't plan to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised, it was always overhyped. At church I'd probably say people were worrying over nothing. I'm not online much, I don't really post anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be glad. My work is about people and paperwork, and if the machines only do a few boring bits, I'm happy to let the younger ones play with them. Nobody in our market town wants to explain their son's disability to a computer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on as I am. Mark, my fiancé, and I are getting married next June, so I'd keep saving for that, about two hundred a month on top of our rent. We've got about three months of savings, which my mother says is sensible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, really. The job is secure, it's a permanent post, and Mark always has work as an electrician. Our worries are normal ones, like the wedding costing more than we planned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're always last to get the hang of the system. Does that ever worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little, when there's a new rollout and my manager watches over my shoulder. But I always get there in the end, and I make fewer mistakes than the quick ones. I'd rather be slow and right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the wedding mean for your plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's at our church, St Anne's, with a lunch in the village hall after. We want children within a couple of years, and I'd like to go part-time when they come. So a steady job matters more than a big job.

say: I'd say AI was always **overhyped**, and people worried over nothing.
I'd say it at church but **not online**, because I rarely post.
think: I'd be **glad** to let younger colleagues handle the few automated bits.
My work is **people and paperwork**, which a computer can't really replace.
do: Keep saving **two hundred a month** for the June wedding.
Keep my **permanent post** and learn the yearly system changes slowly.
feel: **Calm**, with ordinary worries like the wedding costing more than planned.
S0.quote: Nobody in our market town wants to explain their son's disability to a computer.
fieldNote: She takes pride in being **slow and right** rather than quick.
Her plans centre on **marriage and children**, with part-time work later.
She has **never used AI** and sees no reason to start.

steps.text: Keep handling disability and carer's claims as before
Save two hundred a month for the June wedding at St Anne's

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we shouldn't let a program decide who's disabled, that needs a person who's met them. At church I'd say the same, and people there would agree with me. I wouldn't post anything, I'd just grumble at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm worried, because checking evidence and writing decisions is most of what I do between appointments. If they bring in a program, the quick ones will take to it and I won't. I'd be the caseworker who still prints everything while the machine finishes my cases.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my job properly and hope the face-to-face appointments are the part they keep. I'd go to the training if they make me, but I wouldn't volunteer. I'd also put the wedding savings in a separate account and not touch it, in case my hours get cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, if I'm honest. It's like when they changed the system three years ago and I cried in the car park, but worse, because this time it's not just a new screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't volunteer for training. Isn't that a risk, if the quick ones are the ones who stay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I know, Mark says the same. I just don't trust these things, and I don't like learning something that might be gone next year. Maybe I'd go once someone I trust at work says it's actually good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you think decides whether your job stays?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The people in the regional office with their spreadsheets, who've never sat across from a carer. They'd see a cheaper way and take it. I blame them more than the machines.

say: I'd say a **program shouldn't decide** who's disabled without meeting them.
I'd say it at **church** and grumble at home, but never post.
think: Checking evidence and writing decisions is **most of my day**.
The quick colleagues will adapt and **I won't**.
do: Keep doing **face-to-face appointments** and hope that part survives.
Attend training only **if required**, not as a volunteer.
Ring-fence the **wedding savings** in a separate account.
feel: **Worried**, like the system change three years ago, but worse.
S1.quote: I'd be the caseworker who still prints everything while the machine finishes my cases.
fieldNote: She knows **resisting training** puts her at risk but still holds back.
She blames **regional managers** with spreadsheets more than technology.
Her hope rests on **face-to-face work** being protected.

steps.text: Keep running face-to-face appointments with carers
Move wedding savings into a separate untouched account
Wait for a trusted colleague to vouch for training

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's wrong to rush this on families without asking anyone, and I'd write to our local MP, which I've never done. At church people would be frightened, and I'd say we look after each other. At work we'd all be in shock.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd lose my job, I'm sure of it. Nearly everything I do is thinking and paperwork, and the appointments could be done by a screen in the corner. My fiancé Mark keeps his electrician work three years longer than my office job, and I'd feel like the one who let the family down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd make the wedding smaller, just family and the village hall, no band, and save the rest. I'd ask my mum if we could move into her spare room for a year if we had to. I'd look for anything local that's with people, maybe the care home on Bridge Street, even if the pay is less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. I'd be lying awake. I'm not good with change, and two years is no time to become someone else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the care home. Is that something you'd really do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think so, I'm good with people who are struggling. Mark says robots would come for that too in a few years, but a few years is a few years. I'd take it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Mark that first evening?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm sorry, which is silly because it's not my fault. Then I'd ask if we should wait on children. He'd say no, we'll manage, and I'd want to believe him.

say: I'd say it's **wrong to rush** this on families without asking anyone.
I'd **write to our MP** for the first time.
think: I'm sure I'd **lose my job**, since nearly all of it is thinking and paperwork.
Mark keeps his electrician work **three years longer** than me.
do: Shrink the wedding to family and the **village hall**, saving the rest.
Ask my mum about moving into her **spare room** for a year.
Apply to the **care home** on Bridge Street, even for less pay.
feel: Feeling she'd be the one who **let the family down**.
S2.quote: My fiancé Mark keeps his electrician work three years longer than my office job, and I'd feel like the one who let the family down.
fieldNote: She expects to **lose her job** and leans on Mark and her mother.
She feels **guilt** about being the weaker earner, though it isn't her fault.
She picks **care work** for its people contact, accepting robots follow later.

steps.text: Cut the wedding to family and a village hall lunch
Ask her mother about moving into the spare room for a year
Apply for a job at the Bridge Street care home
Write to the local MP about the speed of change

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government has five years, so it should protect jobs like ours and keep people at the front desk. At church I'd say we should pray about it and plan for it, both. I'd still not post anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still expect to lose the office job by 2031, nothing changes that. But five years is enough to have the wedding as we planned it and maybe have a baby while I'm still on proper maternity pay. Five years is long enough to get married properly and short enough that I'd count every month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd keep the wedding as planned, but put more aside afterwards, maybe three hundred a month. I'd wait a year or two to see whether the office actually changes before doing anything drastic. If it does, I'd look at a care qualification, slowly, evenings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy and anxious mixed together. It's still frightening, but I can breathe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait a year or two. What would make you act sooner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If they started a pilot in our office or stopped replacing people who leave. Gillian is retiring next spring, and if they don't fill her post, that tells me everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would it change your plans for children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd try sooner rather than later, so the baby comes while I've still got a job with good maternity pay. My mum would help with childcare. Family is how we'd get through it.

say: I'd say the government should **keep people** at the front desk.
I'd tell church friends to **pray and plan**, both.
think: I'd still lose the office job **by 2031**.
Five years lets us have **the wedding** and maybe a baby on maternity pay.
do: Keep the **wedding as planned**, then save three hundred a month after.
Wait to see whether **Gillian's post** is filled before acting.
Start a **care qualification** slowly in the evenings if the office changes.
feel: **Uneasy and anxious** together, but able to breathe.
S3.quote: Five years is long enough to get married properly and short enough that I'd count every month.
fieldNote: Five years lets her keep **family plans** intact, even speed up a baby.
She watches **a colleague's retirement** as her signal to act.
Her support plan is **family**, especially her mother.

steps.text: Save three hundred a month after the wedding
Watch whether Gillian's post is filled before changing anything
Try for a baby while maternity pay is still secure

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time for the country to sort out proper jobs for people. At church I'd say there's no point panicking. At work I'd say let's see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, I'd probably be at home with small children for some of it anyway. My office job still goes by 2036, but by then I might be part-time or not working. Mark's electrician work would last until about 2039, which is a long time for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much at first, honestly. I'd keep my job, have the wedding, and hope for children in a couple of years. Later, maybe in five or six years, I'd look at what's left, and talk to Mark about whether he could take on an apprentice or I could do his books.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but not frightened. Ten years feels like a long way off when you're planning a wedding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd do his books. Isn't that thinking work that AI takes first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, you're right, I hadn't thought of that. I suppose I'd be helping him run the business in other ways, ringing customers, sorting jobs. I'd have to think about that more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a young person starting in your office in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Get a trade or a job with your hands, and keep your faith and your family close. That's what I'd tell my own children too.

say: I'd say ten years is **plenty of time** to sort out proper jobs.
I'd tell people at church there's **no point panicking**.
think: I might be **at home with children** for part of the decade anyway.
do: Keep my job and **have the wedding**, hoping for children soon.
Revisit in **five or six years** whether I could help with Mark's business.
feel: **Uneasy but not frightened**, since ten years feels far off.
S4.quote: Get a trade or a job with your hands, and keep your faith and your family close.
fieldNote: She leans on a **traditional household plan**, with Mark's trade income lasting longer.
When challenged she admitted **bookkeeping** is exposed too.
She advises young people to choose **trades and family**.

steps.text: Keep the caseworker job through the wedding and first child
Plan for children within a couple of years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because I'm slow to change and there'd be no time. What would help is keeping face-to-face appointments by law for disabled people and carers, and giving staff like me proper time to retrain. I'm good at sitting with a crying carer, and I'd like that to still count for something.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about community. In our town, if the office closes, people will come to church or the post office instead, asking for help with forms. Somebody will still have to help them.

headlineQuote: I'm good at sitting with a crying carer, and I'd like that to still count for something.
portrait: Olga is a **27-year-old caseworker** handling disability and carer's claims in a small market-town office.
She's engaged to Mark, an electrician, and is saving for a **June wedding** at her church.
She **never uses AI** and is slow with new systems, but proud of careful work.
She grows **alarmed** with two years' warning, leaning on family and considering care work.
With longer warning she keeps **family plans** first, counting on Mark's trade lasting longer.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most because she's **slow to change** and there'd be no time.
whatWouldHelp: Keeping **face-to-face appointments** by law for disabled people and carers.
Giving staff like her **proper time** to retrain.
